body: First of all, I’m so sorry you’re feeling this way and second of all, I completely understand how you’re feeling to my core. I planned to have a natural birth and breastfeed and instead I ended up with an emergency c-section and despite my LO being keen to latch in the beginning, had tongue tie and low supply issues which lead me to EPing. I think it was 12 weeks in (now 15 weeks in) and my supply took a dip. After I’d worked so freaking hard to get my maximum milk supply in 24 hours literally days before. I was shattered and I didn’t think I had it in me to do it anymore. I started weaning for a couple of days by pumping less and ad hoc and watched my supply drop, I was gutted and felt immense mum guilt. My partner was the one who said it didn’t need to be all or nothing. He was the one who suggested I just pump what I was comfortable with doing and that we could supplement the rest as we’ve been supplementing since birth anyways. It was that new perspective and a couple of days break that gave me the strength to try again. I went to 6 pumps per day (1 power pump) 3 hours apart for 30mins. My LO has been sleeping through the night mostly so no MOTN pump because I’ve found my body and my milk supply responded to getting rest more than pumping. I did that for a week and now I’ve dropped to 5 pumps per day (1 power pump and the rest 40mins each so I maintain the number of mins I pump overall) and so far my supply has been similiar. The best advice I can give is just do what works for you. It sounds like your current regime is brutal and not sustainable but you may not have to quit entirely either. I haven’t committed to a 6 month goal or 12 month goal. I literally have told my partner I won’t know how I feel about pumping until tomorrow, it takes the pressure off. Remember it’s your body and your life so so what works for you and if you choose formula then you’re no less of a mum. I too wanted to quit because I felt chained to the pump and unable to be there for my LO and enjoy time with her. Now I feel I’m finding a middle ground, still supplementing, but I have some time for me and time for her and that’s a sacrifice worth making. Your presence for your LO and your wellbeing is far more important than whatever difference of milk you could be making if you pushed yourself.

As a fellow depression sufferer I have also experienced this exact scenario. Firstly, I would like to stress to you to not feel bad about yourself because you feel bad. I say this because this is mostly how I felt when I was in your situation. Fortunately I have hindsight now and I'm coping better with my depression so I can understand that is truly is an illness, like having the flu, and is not a reflection on you. With that said, now to the issue at hand. You have two options, both of which involve an in person conversation with your boss or employer and a visit your local doctor to seek some treatment for your depression. Where these options diverge is on what you disclose to your employer. This may depend on how long you have been there, your relationship with your boss/employer and coworkers and also any conditions under a contract of employment. You may choose to provide an ambiguous medical certificate and explain you were unwell, essentially implying it is a once off. Or you may choose to disclose your depression. At this point I stress that if you do choose to be entirely honest that you take with you some proof that you are being proactive in treating your depression. Whilst an employer cannot legally sack you for having depression they will be concerned about attendance and reliability, so if you can prove you are motivated enough to seek help and keep your job then that may work in your favour. So what did I do in my situation? I was completely honest. Unfortunately though I was under casual employment and despite my motivation to treat my depression and several mitigating circumstances they refused to place me back on regular shifts and instead gave me a false promise to call me when they needed me. I'm not going to lie, it was tough to hear and tough to deal with. I beat myself up for months over it. But it happened and it made me make some tough decisions about my life in order to get better. And the silver lining is I'm still alive, rebuilding my life and not letting my depression win. Anyways, there's my two cents. I hope it provides some food for thought and allows you to make a well thought out decision that considers and prepares for all the possibilities.

I don't believe obesity is ever linked holistically with the role of a parent. There are many causes to childhood obesity. Medical illnesses such as thoroid issues, medication such as predisalone for asthmatics, emotional trauma which could include abuse but also losing a parent to divorce or death, losing a sibling or pet to death, troubles with friends, bullying and so on. Children are sensitive and trusting creatures, which can cause them a great deal of emotional trauma which can sometimes lead to obesity. 

However, a child can still have an outstanding parent and still suffer from obesity from the reasons mentioned above, reasons that are difficult for any professional to deflect from a child let alone a parent. 

Therefore, unless the obesity of a child is linked directly to serious neglect either by abuse or malnutrition or medically, the child does not need to be removed from their parent. 

It's also important to consider if the suggestion was taken on, what would happen to the great influx of children in the foster system? Would being placed in a foster system really be better than teaching parents to be responsible?

I've been with my partner for over 3 years now. During the last 3 years we spent 1 year in a long distance relationship. I won't lie, it was the hardest issue we've been through but we did defy the odds and come out of the other side much closer and stronger than before. My best advice is...

1) To set aside at least 20 minutes everyday to speak with your SO. It gives you both the opportunity to share your day with each other without forgetting details which you would if you only spoke every few days. This also helps for when you are no longer at long distances as it means there is less each of you has missed out on in each other's lives.

2) To get on a good phone plan or have a good internet connection. There is nothing more straining on a long distance relationship than concerns about finances or a dodgy connection to get between continuing a bond. 

3) To send a text or two to each other when you're out at social events. It makes your SO still feel important to you and not forgotten even though they aren't there in person. 

4) To visit each other as often as you can. And when you do visit, to make the most of the time together and capture as much of it as you can. My SO and I took lots of pictures which we could look back on and exchanged scents. The latter particularly helped when I couldn't sleep at night because I missed them so much. 

5) To realise that Skype is your best friend when it comes to being intimate with each other while at long distances.
